intro: Four slow notes — C–D–F–E — set Mozart’s last symphonic finale in motion. Bruno Walter conducts the Columbia Symphony Orchestra in a movement whose closing pages fit five separate tunes together.

cues.title: Four long violin notes
cues.text: The first violins play C–D–F–E in long notes. Quicker figures gather around them, and soon different string parts take up the four-note phrase. Its simplicity is useful: Mozart can turn it upside down or place another tune above it, and it remains recognisable.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), IV, opening theme and imitative continuation. K. Dawn Grapes discusses the themes’ contrapuntal treatment: https://fcsymphony.org/mozart-41-jupiter/.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: 10 August in Vienna
cues.text: Mozart dates this symphony 10 August 1788. The E♭ and G minor symphonies have preceded it that summer. For this C major orchestra he adds the trumpets and timpani that the G minor symphony leaves out.
cues.evidence: Date and scoring in the work records for K. 550 and K. 551: https://imslp.org/wiki/Symphony_No.41_in_C_major,_K.551_(Mozart,_Wolfgang_Amadeus) and https://imslp.org/wiki/Symphony_No.40_in_G_minor,_K.550_(Mozart,_Wolfgang_Amadeus).

cues.title: Strings pursue the four notes
cues.text: In the development, the themes pass between parts and through changing keys. A new entry can begin underneath one already in progress. The four long notes give the ear something solid amid the running strings.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), IV, development, bars 158–224.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: C major, with company
cues.text: The violins bring back the opening theme in C major, above moving inner strings. The other parts keep answering and overlapping it. The four-note tune has plenty of company now.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), IV, recapitulation from bar 225.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A letter to Puchberg
cues.text: In Vienna on 27 June 1788, Mozart asks Michael Puchberg for a longer loan. His new rooms are cheaper, and he is working hard, but the bills keep overtaking him. He ends the appeal: “I shall be silent and hope.”
cues.evidence: Mozart to Michael Puchberg, 27 June 1788, Bauer–Deutsch 1079. Our translation of “schweigen und hoffen”: https://dme.mozarteum.at/DME/objs/raradocs/transcr/pdf/BD_1079.pdf.

cues.title: Five tunes at once
cues.text: The coda first turns the four-note idea upside down in a quieter passage. Then Mozart brings five themes together in counterpoint, each with its own rhythm. Long notes, running figures and short replies all fit; the orchestra seems to be finishing several sentences at once.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), IV, bars 357–404. The five-theme combination is described by K. Dawn Grapes, Fort Collins Symphony: https://fcsymphony.org/mozart-41-jupiter/.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Trumpets, drums and C major
cues.text: The running lines converge on the final C major cadences. Trumpets and timpani join the winds and strings in the closing chords. After all those separate voices, everyone has the same last word.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), IV, bars 405–424.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: After the G major cadence
transitions.from: A · Four notes in the violins
transitions.to: Dev · The four notes change hands
transitions.how: The exposition closes in G major. In the quieter opening of the development, the strings take familiar figures into new keys. Entries overlap and repeat at different pitches, loosening the hold of the G major cadence.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), IV, bars 151–169.

transitions.title: G in the bass prepares C
transitions.from: Dev · The four notes change hands
transitions.to: A′ · The violins recover C major
transitions.how: The development settles on the dominant of C major, with G in the bass. The violins restore C–D–F–E above the moving inner strings. The long notes recover their opening key while the accompaniment keeps its quick pulse.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), IV, bars 219–233.

transitions.title: The four notes turn upside down
transitions.from: A′ · The violins recover C major
transitions.how: A C major close is followed by a quieter passage in which the four-note theme turns upside down. The strings begin the final contrapuntal build from these sustained notes, adding the quicker themes one by one before the full orchestra confirms C major.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), IV, bars 355–383: coda from bar 357, inversion from bar 361, contrapuntal combination from bar 372.

source.locator: IV. Molto allegro, PDF pp. 35–56, bars 1–424: four-note theme, development, return and contrapuntal coda.

timeline.note: First violins play C–D–F–E above moving second violins; lower strings join as the phrase expands.
The full orchestra answers, with trumpets and timpani reinforcing the strings.
Strings begin the development above held horn notes; woodwinds rejoin as the phrases continue.
Woodwinds and strings pass the themes between them, punctuated by horns, trumpets and timpani.
The opening theme returns above moving inner strings; winds, brass and timpani join its continuation.
Full orchestral phrases alternate with lighter passages of interweaving strings and winds.
A full orchestral phrase opens the coda, then the players fall quiet.
Sustained string and flute notes reveal the four-note theme turned upside down.
The themes combine in the strings, with winds, brass and timpani joining the final build.

composer.background:
When Leopold Mozart arrived in Vienna on 11 February 1785, the copyist was still writing out his son’s new concerto for that evening’s concert at the Mehlgrube. Wolfgang had been so busy supervising the copying that he had found no time to try the finale through. This was K. 466 in D minor: restless, syncopated strings, then a piano entering with a tune of its own. Leopold thought the concert splendid.

The next day, Haydn heard three quartets at Wolfgang’s home. Leopold recorded his verdict in a letter to Nannerl begun on 14 February: “Before God, and as an honest man, I tell you that your son is the greatest composer I know, personally or by name.” Haydn praised his taste and his knowledge of composition. Mozart would dedicate the quartets to him.
